WOKE LEAN

Scarface

Scarface is a great film that is telling you a lie about itself.

Full analysis below
Film · Theatrical June 9, 2026 Analyzed by Debra Ducane 15 min read
Woke Score
18.38

✅ NOT A WOKE TRAP

Scarface does not qualify as a woke trap under VVWS v1.1. A woke trap requires woke content hidden past the 50% runtime mark. Scarface announces its ideology from the opening frame. The film is a 170-minute immersion in criminal excess that glorifies Tony Montana's rise while superficially condemning his fall. The woke signals, primarily the glamorization of crime and the anti-establishment American Dream critique via criminal protagonist, are front and center throughout. Nothing is concealed. The WOKE LEAN verdict at -3 accurately reflects a film that is morally complex but ultimately tilted toward the woke column by its structural glorification of criminality and Oliver Stone's anti-capitalist authorial framework.

Our Verdict on Scarface

Scarface is a great film that is telling you a lie about itself.

The lie is this: the film claims to be a cautionary tale about the self-destruction that follows greed and excess. Tony Montana wants the world and everything in it, gets it, and is destroyed by it. Lesson delivered. But for 150 of its 170 minutes, Scarface makes Tony Montana look cooler than anyone you have ever met. Brian De Palma and cinematographer John Alonzo photograph his mansion, his cars, his suits, his cocaine mountain, and his pool like they are the most desirable things on earth. Giorgio Moroder's synth score makes every scene feel like the apex of glamorous experience. And Al Pacino plays Tony with a ferocious charisma that makes you root for him even as he does the things you should not root for.

That is the film's problem and its fascination, and it is why Scarface has become one of the most culturally persistent films of the past half century while also being a film that does not, on honest analysis, say what it claims to say.

Oliver Stone wrote the script while using cocaine heavily, and it shows. Tony Montana is Stone's id at full volume: an immigrant outsider who looked at America's capitalism and concluded correctly that its rules exist to keep people like him outside, and who decided to ignore those rules. Stone's target is the American economic system. His argument is that the difference between Tony Montana and a legitimate Miami businessman is not moral but procedural. Both men want to accumulate wealth and power. Tony is honest about the methods.

This is a woke reading of the American Dream, and it is embedded in the film's structure. The film's most explicitly political moment comes when Tony confronts a restaurant full of rich people and screams at them: 'You need people like me. You need people like me so you can point your fingers and say that's the bad guy.' He is, in Oliver Stone's moral universe, correct. The legitimate economy produced him by excluding him. He took the available route. The system that condemns him is the same system that created him.

There are genuine traditional elements in Scarface, and they matter. The most important is family. Tony Montana's relationship with his mother and sister is the film's moral anchor, such as it is. His love for Gina is possessive and complicated, shading into something the film hints at but does not quite name. But the love itself is real. He wanted to bring his mother out of poverty. He wanted to protect Gina from the world he inhabits. When Manny, his best friend, secretly marries Gina, Tony kills him out of jealousy and then kills Gina when she tells him what he's done. The destruction of family is the final cost of Tony's choices, and it lands with genuine moral weight.

The other traditional element is consequences. Tony does die at the end. He does reap what he sowed. His cocaine addiction destroys him before the gunmen do. The final sequence, Tony defending his fortress alone after driving away everyone who cared about him, is genuinely tragic and not ironic about its tragedy. Say what you will about Scarface's glorification problem: the film does not let Tony Montana win. He loses everything, including the things that actually mattered.

But the film's trad signals are outweighed by its structural problems. A film can have consequences without having moral clarity, and Scarface does not have moral clarity. The difference between The Godfather and Scarface is that The Godfather mourns what crime does to family. Scarface mourns Tony's fall but is unable to stop finding him magnificent. The 170-minute runtime is largely spent in admiration of the man it claims to be warning against.

For VirtueVigil readers, the WOKE LEAN verdict comes down to this: Scarface is a film whose surface moral (crime doesn't pay) is undercut by its structural glorification of the criminal, whose celebration of excess is more convincing than its condemnation of it, and whose ideological author, Oliver Stone, embedded a critique of American capitalism that is not conservative in any meaningful sense. The traditional elements, consequences, family violated and mourned, masculine code of loyalty, are real but outweighed. Tony Montana dies. He should have. The film just makes you wish he hadn't.

Creative Team Deep Dive

Director: Brian De Palma

MIXED LEANING WOKE. De Palma's career is defined by a tension between formal virtuosity and ideological content. Carrie (1976) is a film about female rage and institutional cruelty. Dressed to Kill (1980) provoked feminist criticism for its violence against women. Blow Out (1981) is a paranoid anti-institutional thriller about the machinery of political cover-up. Scarface is his most commercially successful film and his most ideologically complex. The Untouchables (1987) is genuinely heroic and traditional. Carlito's Way (1993) is a crime film with conservative undertones. De Palma himself is on record as a formalist first: technique is his primary interest, not politics. He has described Scarface as a critique of the cocaine era's materialism. Whether the film achieves that critique or inadvertently celebrates what it claims to condemn is the central question of any honest analysis. The answer is complicated, which is why this is WOKE LEAN rather than WOKE.

Brian De Palma was born in Newark in 1940 and emerged from the New Hollywood generation alongside Coppola, Scorsese, and Spielberg. His technical influences are Hitchcock and the French New Wave, and his films are marked by elaborate set pieces, operatic violence, and a camera that calls attention to itself as a formal instrument. Scarface was a risky project when Universal approved it in 1982: a three-hour R-rated crime epic written by Oliver Stone and starring Al Pacino speaking in a Cuban accent, depicting cocaine trafficking with explicit detail. The original 1932 Howard Hawks film was a Prohibition-era gangster picture operating under the Production Code. De Palma and Stone's version dispensed with the Code's requirements for explicit moral condemnation and made a film that trusts, or at least hopes, that the audience will see Tony Montana's destruction as judgment rather than endorsement. Whether that trust was warranted depends on which audience you are describing. The film was received with largely negative critical reviews at release, dismissed as excessive and morally irresponsible. Over the following decade it became one of the most-watched films in VHS history and arguably the most culturally influential crime film of the 1980s, generating an entire visual and lyrical vocabulary for hip-hop culture's engagement with excess, ambition, and the cost of those things.

Content Breakdown

Adult Viewer Insight

Scarface rewards revisiting as a document of a cultural moment. The cocaine economy of early 1980s Miami was real and it did produce men like Tony Montana. Oliver Stone's critique of the relationship between the legitimate and criminal economies is not without merit as social observation, even if the conclusions he draws from it are progressive in the worst sense. The film's most honest scene is not the mansion massacre but the quiet moment where Tony looks at his 'the world is yours' globe and knows it isn't. He is in a room that contains everything he said he wanted, and none of it has filled the vacancy that drove him to get it. That is a traditional insight: the vacancy that ambition cannot fill is spiritual, not material. Scarface gets to that insight and then does not know what to do with it, because Stone's ideological framework does not have a category for spiritual solutions.

Parental Guidance

Rated R, 17+. Scarface is one of the most extreme R-rated films ever produced: extreme graphic violence including a chainsaw murder and a mansion massacre, pervasive cocaine use depicted in a glamorous visual context, strong sexual content, and hundreds of profanities across a 170-minute runtime. The film's cautionary intent is real but undermined by its visual language, and teenage viewers are far more likely to absorb the style than the lesson. Not appropriate for anyone under 17. Adult viewers should approach it as the morally complex object it is: a technically brilliant, ideologically compromised film that tells you one thing while showing you another.
